payload.explanation: range(1, n) stops before n, so the loop never adds n itself; it should be range(1, n + 1).
if (n = 0) assigns 0 to n instead of comparing, so n is always reset to 0 and the function incorrectly returns false for every input.
The query aliases the result as cheapest but uses MAX(price), which returns the most expensive product instead of the least expensive one; it should use MIN(price).
if (b < max) only updates max when b is smaller, so it never captures the larger value; the comparison should be b > max.
The loop condition i <= nums.length lets i reach nums.length, an out-of-bounds index that is undefined, turning total into NaN.
manager_id = NULL never evaluates to true because comparisons with NULL always yield unknown; the query should use manager_id IS NULL instead.
i <= scores.length lets i reach 3, which is out of bounds for a 3-element array and throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; the condition should be i < scores.length.
age is an int, so concatenating it directly with strings raises a TypeError; it needs to be converted with str(age) or an f-string.
The function computes n * 2 but never returns it, so double(5) evaluates to undefined instead of 10.
GROUP BY id groups by the unique primary key instead of customer_id, so each group has only one row and SUM(amount) never combines a customer's orders.
total / count performs integer division and truncates to 3 before being assigned to the double, so average prints 3.0 instead of 3.5; it needs a cast such as (double) total / count.
range(1, len(nums) + 1) lets i reach len(nums), which is one past the last valid index and raises an IndexError on nums[i].
Array.sort() without a comparator sorts elements as strings, so it orders numbers lexicographically instead of numerically; it needs (a, b) => a - b.
HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 keeps emails that appear exactly once, the opposite of the duplicates the comment asks for; it should be HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.

input == "yes" compares object references, and since input was created with new String(...), it is a different object from the literal, so the comparison is false even though the text matches; the fix is input.equals("yes").
The recursive call decrements n by 2 instead of 1, so for odd inputs it skips over the n == 0 base case and recurses forever.
The callback passed to setInterval is a regular function, so this inside it no longer refers to the Counter instance; it should be an arrow function to keep this bound to the instance.
A plain JOIN excludes customers with no matching orders, such as Sam, even though the comment asks for every customer; it should be a LEFT JOIN.
The loop starts at i = 3 instead of i = 2, so it never tests divisibility by 2, making isPrime(4) incorrectly return true.

def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket
first = add_item("apple")
second = add_item("banana")
print(second)
payload.explanation: The default argument basket=[] is created once and reused across every call, so items from earlier calls leak into later ones; it should default to None and build a new list inside the function.
var i is function-scoped and shared by every closure, so by the time the callbacks run they all read the final value 3 instead of each capturing its own loop index.
The JOIN to order_items multiplies each order row by its number of items before the SUM runs, so an order with more than one item has its amount counted multiple times.
a == b compares object references for boxed Integers, and 200 falls outside the cached -128 to 127 range, so the two boxed values are different objects; the comparison should use a.equals(b).
n += 1 increases n instead of decreasing it, so the condition n > 0 never becomes false and the loop runs forever.
